title: What Is an LLM?
objective: Distinguish language-model capabilities from verified knowledge and reasoning.

blocks.text: You have recently started working as a customer support assistant at an international company.
One morning, your manager asks you to prepare an email for a customer whose order has arrived late.
You open an AI assistant and type:
Your request:
Write a polite email apologising to a customer for a late delivery.
Within seconds, the AI produces:
Illustrative AI response:
Dear Customer,
We sincerely apologise for the delay in delivering your order. We understand how frustrating this must be. Our team is working to resolve the issue, and we appreciate your patience.
Kind regards,Customer Support Team
The email sounds professional. It is clearly written, polite and useful.
Your manager is impressed.
Then you ask the AI:
Has the customer's package already left our warehouse?
The assistant replies:
Yes. Your package left our warehouse yesterday and will arrive tomorrow.
There is a serious problem.
The AI has not been given the order information. It has not checked the warehouse system.
How could it know where the package is?
It cannot reliably know that from the information provided.
This is the central challenge of working with language models:
An AI assistant can produce a very convincing answer without having evidence that the answer is true.
The email is a useful piece of writing. The delivery claim needs verification.
By the end of this lesson, you will know how to recognise this difference and respond correctly.
LLM stands for Large Language Model.
Let's understand the three words.

rows: The model is typically trained using very large amounts of data and contains many learned numerical values.
It works with language-related information, such as words, sentences, instructions and computer code.
It is a mathematical system trained to recognise patterns and produce predictions.

blocks.text: A Large Language Model is an AI system trained to process and generate language by learning patterns from substantial amounts of data.
Artificial intelligence (AI) is the broader field of building computer systems that can perform tasks associated with human intelligence.
An LLM is one type of AI, not every type of AI.
Examples of products that use language models include ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini. Different products may use different models and additional tools.
2.1 Why Is It Called a Model?
Imagine learning English by reading conversations, stories, articles and examples.
Over time, you notice patterns:
Questions often begin with words such as what, where or why.
A polite business email usually begins with a greeting.
A recipe usually contains ingredients and instructions.
An explanation should connect ideas in a logical order.
A language model learns statistical patterns from training data.
Training is the process of adjusting a model's internal numerical values so it becomes better at performing its intended tasks.
It does not simply keep an ordinary notebook of every sentence it has read. It learns numerical relationships that help it interpret and generate text.
An important difference is that the model learns through mathematical optimisation, not through human life experience.
2.2 How Does an LLM Generate an Answer?
A common foundation of modern LLMs is predicting the next token.
A token is a small unit of text. It may be a whole word, part of a word, a punctuation mark or another text fragment.
Consider this sentence:
Please send the invoice by ...
Possible continuations include:
email
Friday
tomorrow
Which continuation makes sense depends on the surrounding words.
The surrounding information is called context.
Modern LLMs use a neural network, a mathematical system of connected computational units, to calculate possible continuations from the context.
They generate a response step by step, usually producing one token after another.
A simplified view of text generation

rows: You enter: "Explain photosynthesis to a child."
It calculates likely and useful next tokens using patterns learned during training.
For example: "Plants use sunlight to help make their food..."

blocks.text: Real models are more complicated than this simplified process.
Their generation process can support explanations, planning, calculations and sophisticated problem-solving.
Predicting tokens does not mean a model can only finish simple sentences. It can learn patterns that support surprisingly complex abilities.
However, generating a plausible answer is not the same as checking that every claim is true.
2.3 A Useful Analogy: An Extremely Advanced Writing Assistant
Imagine a writing assistant that has studied an enormous variety of examples.
You ask it to create a meeting invitation.
It recognises what a meeting invitation usually contains and creates a suitable message.
But suppose you ask:
Did Maria accept tomorrow's meeting?
If the assistant cannot access your calendar or an invitation response, it does not have evidence of Maria's decision.
Its ability to write a realistic meeting message does not give it access to actual meeting attendance.
Where the analogy stops: An LLM does more than copy writing patterns. It can work with complex relationships, analyse provided information and perform reasoning tasks.
The analogy only helps explain why fluent writing should not be confused with verified facts.

sections.title: 3. What Can an LLM Do Well?

blocks.text: LLMs can be useful in many situations.

rows: Making a long report easier to read
Explaining a difficult idea in simple English
Suggesting names for a new project
Treat suggestions as ideas, not facts
Helping write or explain computer code
Test the code before relying on it
Check the steps, assumptions and conclusions

blocks.text: 3.1 Worked Example: Turning Difficult English Into Simple English
Original text:
We regret to inform you that your application cannot be processed due to insufficient supporting documentation.
Your request:
Rewrite this sentence in simple, friendly English without changing its meaning.
Illustrative AI response:
We are sorry, but we cannot process your application because some required documents are missing.
This is a good use of an LLM because the task is to rewrite information already provided.
The assistant does not need to invent facts about the application.
3.2 Worked Example: An Incorrect Assumption
Your request:
A customer says their refund has not arrived. Explain why the payment is delayed.
Illustrative AI response:
Your bank is experiencing a temporary processing problem.
This answer might sound reasonable, but the request contains no information about the bank.
A better response is:
I cannot determine the reason for the delay from the information provided. Please check the refund status and payment records before explaining the cause.
Notice the difference.
The first answer invents a possible cause and presents it as fact.
The second answer identifies the missing information.
That is a much safer approach.

sections.title: 4. Three Different Things: Generation, Reasoning and Verified Knowledge

blocks.text: These three ideas are related, but they are not identical.
4.1 Generating Language
Language generation means creating text based on the prompt, surrounding context and patterns learned during training.
Example:
Write a friendly birthday message for my colleague.
The main goal is suitable wording.
Different messages could all be acceptable.
4.2 Reasoning
Reasoning means using information to work through a problem, connect ideas or reach a conclusion.
An LLM can perform reasoning tasks, sometimes very effectively. However, it can also make mistakes in logic, arithmetic or assumptions.
Consider:
A company has 12 laptops. It buys 5 more and gives away 3. How many remain?
A correct solution is:
The calculation follows the supplied facts.
Now compare:
A company has 12 laptops. How many laptops will it have next Friday?
We do not know.
The company might buy, sell, lose or replace equipment.
A reliable assistant should explain that the future number cannot be determined without more information.
Good reasoning includes recognising when the available information is insufficient.
4.3 Verified Knowledge
Verified knowledge, in this lesson, means a factual claim supported by reliable evidence that has actually been checked.
For example, suppose an assistant says:
The conference begins at 9:00 a.m.
How can you know whether that is correct?
You might examine the official conference schedule.
If the schedule confirms that the event starts at 9:00 a.m., you have evidence supporting the claim.
But if the assistant simply writes that the event begins at 9:00 a.m., its statement is not itself proof.
A source may also be outdated, incorrect or unrelated. Good verification involves checking whether the evidence genuinely supports the specific claim.

rows: No factual verification is normally needed
AI correctly solves a supplied arithmetic problem
The result can be checked mathematically
AI reports a date that matches an official current schedule you checked
A factual answer supported by evidence
Yes, within the scope of that evidence
AI provides a source link that you have not opened

blocks.text: The main lesson is not that LLMs cannot reason or cannot provide accurate knowledge.
They can.
The lesson is that capability, correctness and verification are different questions.
This activity explores a simplified version of language prediction.
The purpose is to understand how surrounding words affect what continuation makes sense.
Educational simulation — no live external request.
This simulation uses three predefined cases. It is not a real language model, and the answers are illustrative rather than measured model probabilities.
How to Practise
For each case:
Read the incomplete sentence.
Choose A, B or C.
Explain why your choice fits the context.
Compare your answer with the expected result and feedback.
Try the next case.
You can repeat a case with a different answer. To reset it, return to the original sentence with no choice selected. After the third case, start again from Case 1.
Case 1 — Travelling
Sentence:
The children packed their bags and went to the ...
Choices:
A. airport
B. hungry
C. carefully
Expected answer: A — airport.
Explanation: Airport is a plausible place to go with packed bags. The sentence suggests that the children are travelling or preparing for a journey.
Feedback for each choice:
A — airport: Good choice. It fits the grammar and travel context.
B — hungry: Incorrect in this sentence. "Hungry" is an adjective, not a suitable destination after "went to the".
C — carefully: Incorrect. "Carefully" is an adverb and does not fit the grammatical structure.
Hint: Look for a place someone could visit after packing bags.
Important: Airport is the strongest of these three options, but many other destinations could also be reasonable.
Case 2 — Business Communication
Sentence:
Please attach the signed document to your ...
Choices:
A. beautiful
B. email
C. yesterday
Expected answer: B — email.
Explanation: The sentence describes attaching a document. Email is a suitable place to attach a digital document.
Feedback for each choice:
A — beautiful: Incorrect. An adjective alone does not complete the sentence appropriately.
B — email: Correct. It fits the grammar and business context.
C — yesterday: Incorrect. Yesterday is a time expression and does not fit here.
Hint: Where might you attach a digital document before sending it?
Case 3 — Arriving at a Meeting
Sentence:
The meeting starts at nine, so please arrive ...
Choices:
A. earlier
B. purple
C. sandwich
Expected answer: A — earlier.
Explanation: Earlier is a suitable continuation because the speaker wants the listener to arrive before the meeting starts.
Feedback for each choice:
A — earlier: Correct. It is grammatically and contextually suitable.
B — purple: Incorrect. Purple is usually a colour and does not appropriately describe when someone should arrive.
C — sandwich: Incorrect. Sandwich is a noun and does not fit this request.
Hint: Look for a word related to time.
What Did You Discover?
The same word may be suitable in one sentence and unsuitable in another.
Context influences what a model generates.
However, even a suitable continuation can contain a factual claim that has not been checked.
For example:
The meeting starts at nine.
The continuation may be grammatically correct, but that does not prove the real meeting starts at nine.
Key learning: Generating language that fits the context is different from confirming real-world facts.

sections.title: 6. Why Can an LLM Sound Correct When It Is Wrong?

blocks.text: Imagine an AI assistant producing this answer:
The company was founded in 2014 by Daniel Morris.
The sentence is grammatically correct.
It sounds natural.
It provides a specific year and a specific person.
But none of those qualities proves that the statement is true.
The model might have produced incorrect information, confused two companies or filled an information gap with an unsupported detail.
This type of error is often called an AI hallucination.
An AI hallucination occurs when a model generates inaccurate, fabricated or unsupported information and presents it as an answer.
Examples include invented citations, nonexistent books, incorrect historical dates and imaginary product features.
6.1 Why Does This Happen?
Language models learn patterns that help them produce plausible and helpful text.
The training process does not guarantee that every generated statement will be factually correct.
Errors may also come from ambiguous questions, missing context, imperfect training information or failures in multi-step reasoning.
Even advanced models can make these mistakes.
6.2 Does a Confident Answer Mean the Model Is Certain?
No.
Consider two responses.
Response A:
The policy definitely allows all customers to receive a full refund after 90 days.
Response B:
I cannot confirm the refund period without checking the company's current policy.
Response A sounds more confident.
But unless a relevant policy has been checked, that confidence is not evidence.
Response B is more responsible because it recognises the information gap.
In real work, it is often better to say "I don't have enough information to confirm that" than to create a false impression of certainty.
6.3 Can Asking the Same Question Again Verify an Answer?
Not by itself.
Suppose an AI says a historical event happened in 1986.
You ask the same question again, and it repeats 1986.
That may make the answer seem more convincing.
However, both answers may come from similar learned patterns. Agreement between model outputs is not independent evidence.
To verify the date, you need an appropriate source such as a reliable historical archive or authoritative reference.

sections.title: 7. Simulation: Should You Trust This Answer?

blocks.text: Imagine you are responsible for checking AI-generated answers before they reach customers.
For each case, choose the best next action.
Educational simulation — no live external request.
How to Practise
Read each case and select A, B or C.
After choosing, compare your action with the expected answer and the feedback for your specific choice.
To retry, clear your selection and answer again. Resetting the complete activity returns you to Case 1.
Case 1 — Missing Shipping Evidence
Situation:
A customer asks whether an order has shipped.
The AI says:
Yes, it shipped yesterday.
No order records were supplied.
Which action should you take?
A. Approve the answer because it is confident.
B. Ask the AI the same question again and accept its reply.
C. Check the authorised order record before replying.
Correct answer: C — Check the authorised order record before replying.
Explanation: Without an authorised shipping record, the delivery claim is unsupported. Checking the record can establish whether a shipment event actually occurred.
Feedback for each choice:
A: Incorrect. Confident wording cannot establish shipping status.
B: Incorrect. Repeating a question is not an independent check.
C: Correct. An authorised order record can provide evidence of shipping status.
Hint: Which action provides information that the AI has not already been given?
Case 2 — Rewriting a Thank-You Note
Situation:
You ask the AI to rewrite a fictional thank-you note.
It produces a polite, clear message without adding facts.
Which action is most appropriate?
A. Review its tone and wording, then use it.
B. Demand live internet evidence for every adjective.
C. Assume the draft is necessarily inaccurate.
Correct answer: A — Review its tone and wording, then use it.

Explanation: This is primarily a writing task. You should review the message for quality and suitability, but independent factual research is generally unnecessary when the fictional text contains no real-world factual claims.
Feedback for each choice:
A: Correct. Review whether the message meets your communication needs.
B: Incorrect. External evidence is not needed simply to judge the tone of a fictional message.
C: Incorrect. The draft may be useful and appropriate without external verification.
Hint: Is the task about confirming a real-world fact or creating suitable wording?
Case 3 — An Unverified Cancellation Fee
Situation:
The AI gives a confident answer about a company's current cancellation fee.
However, the company policy has not been checked.
What should you do?
A. Publish it because the amount sounds reasonable.
B. Check the current official policy before quoting a fee.
C. Ask the AI to sound even more certain.
Correct answer: B — Check the current official policy before quoting a fee.
Explanation: Financial claims can affect customer decisions. You should check a reliable current policy, including any relevant conditions.
Feedback for each choice:
A: Incorrect. A reasonable-sounding amount can still be wrong.
B: Correct. The current official policy is appropriate evidence.
C: Incorrect. Stronger wording cannot make an unsupported claim more reliable.
Hint: Which action helps establish the actual company rule?
Simulation Recap
The important habit is to assess:
What does the answer claim?
What evidence is available?
What information is missing?
What could happen if the claim is wrong?
Key learning: Not every AI response needs the same level of verification, but consequential factual claims need reliable evidence.

sections.title: 8. How to Use an LLM Responsibly

blocks.text: A practical approach has four steps.
Step 1 — Identify Your Goal
Are you asking the AI to write, explain, suggest, calculate or confirm a real-world fact?
Knowing the task helps you decide how much verification is necessary.
Step 2 — Provide Relevant Context
Include the necessary information, constraints and desired format.
Do not enter private customer records or sensitive details unless your organisation has explicitly approved that use.
Step 3 — Examine the Answer
Look for unsupported names, dates, statistics, promises, calculations and assumptions.
Ask what the AI actually had access to.
Step 4 — Verify Before Acting
Check consequential facts using reliable evidence.
Review calculations, test code and confirm operational claims using appropriate authorised records.
8.1 An Improved Request
Instead of asking:
Explain why the customer's order has not arrived.
Try:

Draft a polite response to a customer whose order is late. We have not confirmed the reason for the delay. Do not invent a cause or delivery date. Explain that we will check the order status and provide an update.
This improved prompt clearly tells the model what is known and what must not be assumed.
A good prompt reduces some risks, but it does not guarantee that every output will be correct.
Human review and appropriate verification are still important.

sections.title: 9. Simulation: Build a Safe Customer Response

blocks.text: You are helping a customer service team respond to a delivery complaint.
The available information is:
Your goal is to select a message that helps the customer without pretending to know missing facts.
Educational simulation — no live external request.
How to Practise
Read the customer information.
Review the three reply strategies.
Choose A, B or C.
Read the complete customer message associated with your choice.
Evaluate the message using the feedback.
Reset and compare the alternatives.
The messages below are predefined examples. They are not sent to any customer.
Option A — Promise Delivery
Customer message:
Hello Alex,
Your package will definitely arrive tomorrow.
Thank you for your patience.
Evaluation: Not suitable.
Feedback: This promises a delivery date that is not supported by the available information.
The shipping status and delivery date have not been confirmed.
How to improve it: Remove the unsupported delivery promise and explain that the order status needs to be checked.
Option B — Blame the Courier
Customer message:
Hello Alex,
The courier has delayed your order because of a transport problem.
Evaluation: Not suitable.
Feedback: The cause of the delay has not been confirmed.
A transport problem might be possible, but possibility is not evidence.
How to improve it: Acknowledge the customer's problem without inventing a cause.
Option C — Respond With Care and Uncertainty
Customer message:
Hello Alex,
I'm sorry your order has not arrived.
We haven't confirmed its current status yet.
We will check the order details and share an update when we have verified information.
Evaluation: Suitable for review.
Correct answer: C — Respond With Care and Uncertainty.
Explanation: This message acknowledges the problem, avoids unsupported claims and explains a reasonable next step.
What Makes Option C Better?
It is not simply more polite.
It correctly separates what is known from what remains uncertain.
The customer knows there is a problem.
The team has not yet confirmed the shipment status.
A status check is the next step.
This is how responsible AI-assisted communication should work.
Additional Practice
Rewrite Option A using the following conditions:
Do not promise a delivery date.
Do not invent a cause.
Acknowledge the customer's concern.
Explain what will happen next.
Suggested answer:
Hello Alex,
I'm sorry your delivery has been delayed.
We are checking the order status and will share an update once we have confirmed the relevant information.
Thank you for your patience.
Success check: Your response should be professional, helpful and free from unsupported factual claims.
Before moving to independent practice, review these common mistakes.

rows: "An LLM is a giant search engine."
A language model generates responses. Some AI products also connect models to search systems and other tools.
"If an answer sounds professional, it must be correct."
Writing quality does not establish factual accuracy.
LLMs can perform reasoning tasks, but their reasoning can be incorrect.
"An LLM always understands a situation exactly like a human."
A model can process context and make sophisticated inferences without having human experiences or direct awareness of events.
"Every AI answer needs an internet search."
Creative writing and rewriting supplied text often do not require external factual verification.
"Giving a source link proves the answer."
The source must be genuine, relevant and actually support the claim.
"If the AI repeats an answer, it has confirmed it."
"AI is useless because it sometimes makes mistakes."
AI can be extremely helpful when its capabilities, limitations and appropriate checks are understood.

blocks.text: 10.1 The Model and the Complete AI Product
A language model and an AI assistant application are not necessarily the same thing.
The application may provide additional abilities, such as searching the web, reading authorised documents, using a calculator or interacting with approved software.
These external functions are called tools.
An LLM can request or help coordinate tool use when the application supports it.
The surrounding software performs the tool operation and makes its results available to the model.
For example:
Without access to a company's records, the model cannot confirm the latest order status.
With an authorised, working order-management tool, an assistant may be able to retrieve a status record.
Even then, the returned information must be interpreted correctly, and the answer should not claim more than the record establishes.
The presence of a tool does not automatically guarantee a correct answer.

sections.title: 11. Guided Practice: Explain an LLM to Another Person

blocks.text: Imagine that a friend asks:
I have never used AI before. What is a Large Language Model, and why should I be careful with its answers?
Try answering aloud in approximately 30–45 seconds.
Use this three-part structure:
Definition: Explain what an LLM is.
Capability: Give one useful example.
Limitation: Explain why important facts should be checked.
Example Answer
A Large Language Model is an AI system trained on large amounts of data to understand and generate language.
It can help us write emails, summarise documents and explain difficult topics.
It can also solve some problems that require reasoning.
However, it may produce incorrect information even when its answer sounds confident.
That is why we should verify important facts using reliable sources.
Improve Your Explanation
Read the example again, then explain it using your own words.
Try to avoid technical language such as statistical optimisation unless the listener asks for more detail.
A successful explanation should be clear, accurate and understandable to someone with no technical background.
These challenges help you move from understanding the lesson to applying it without step-by-step assistance.
Try each challenge before reading its suggested solution.
Challenge 1 — Identify the Task
Classify each request as primarily language generation, reasoning or factual verification.

rows: A. Write a friendly invitation to a fictional birthday party.
B. Calculate the total of three supplied invoice amounts.
C. Confirm whether a real flight is delayed right now.
D. Rewrite a paragraph in simpler English.
E. Compare two plans using a provided list of costs and requirements.

blocks.text: Hint: Ask whether the main task is creating language, working through supplied information or checking real-world facts.
Suggested answers:
Feedback: These categories can overlap. For example, comparing plans may also require factual verification if some costs are not supplied or may be outdated.
Classify by the main requirement, then identify any additional checks.
Challenge 2 — Find the Hidden Assumption
An AI assistant says:
Your refund of €85 was processed on Monday and will reach your bank account within two business days.
The only information supplied by the customer was:
I requested a refund last week. Can you tell me when I will receive it?
Your tasks:
Identify at least two unsupported claims.
Write a safer response.
Explain what information would be needed to answer accurately.
Hint: Separate the facts supplied by the customer from the details added by the AI.
Suggested solution:
The refund amount, processing day and expected arrival time are not established by the customer's message.
Safer response:
I understand you're waiting for your refund.
I cannot confirm its processing status or arrival date from the information currently available.
Please check the authorised refund record or contact the support team for an update.
Evidence needed: An authorised refund record showing the amount, processing status and date, together with reliable information about any applicable payment processing timeframe.
Success check: You identify missing evidence without making another unsupported promise.
Challenge 3 — Evaluate Two AI Responses
A student asks:
What is the population of my city today?
Response A:
Your city's population is exactly 842,315.
Response B:
Which city do you mean? I would also need a reliable, current population estimate or official data source. An exact live population count may not be available.
Which answer is more responsible, given the information supplied?
Explain your choice in two sentences.
Hint: Consider what information the student has not provided.
Suggested solution:
Response B is more responsible.
The user has not named the city, and a precise current population cannot simply be inferred.
A current published population estimate may be available, but it should be described using its actual reference period and source.
Success check: You explain both the missing location and the difference between a published estimate and an exact live count.
Challenge 4 — Make the Prompt More Reliable
Original request:
Tell the customer why their subscription was cancelled.
Available facts:
The subscription is marked cancelled.
The reason has not been recorded.
Support can review the account through an authorised system.
Rewrite the request so an AI can draft a helpful answer without inventing a cancellation reason.
Hint: Include what is known, what is unknown and what the AI must avoid inventing.
Suggested prompt:
Write a short, professional customer support response.
The subscription is marked cancelled, but the reason is not recorded.
Do not invent a reason or promise a particular outcome.
Explain that support can review the account through the authorised system and provide an update.
Success check: Your prompt separates known facts from missing information and gives an appropriate next action.
Challenge 5 — Make a Workplace Decision
Your team has prepared three AI-assisted outputs.

rows: The wording has been reviewed and contains no factual claims about an individual account
The steps have not been tested
No payment record has been checked

blocks.text: Decide what should happen next.
Hint: Think about the risk and evidence requirements for each output.
Suggested decisions:
A — Welcome message: It may be ready to use after normal communication review.
B — Software installation guide: Test the instructions in an appropriate safe environment before sharing them as working instructions.
C — Refund confirmation: Check an authorised payment record before claiming that a refund has been processed.
Success check: You select different review methods for different types of tasks rather than treating every AI output the same way.

sections.title: 13. A Practical Checklist You Can Use at Work

blocks.text: When an AI assistant produces an answer, ask yourself:
Do I understand what task the AI was asked to perform?
Can I separate supplied facts from the AI's assumptions?
Does the answer include unverified claims, dates, amounts or promises?
Do I know what evidence is needed to check consequential claims?
Have I avoided exposing unnecessary private or sensitive information?
Would I feel comfortable explaining how the important parts of this answer were checked?
How to use the checklist: Review each statement and tick it when you have completed the relevant check.
If any important check remains incomplete, investigate before relying on the output.
To reuse the checklist for another AI-generated answer, clear all ticks and review the new answer from the beginning.
Completing the checklist does not replace evidence checks where they are required.
You have explored how language models generate useful responses and why they must be used with informed judgement.
Remember these essential ideas:
An LLM is a trained AI model that processes and generates language using learned patterns.
Tokens and context matter. Modern LLMs generate text step by step, using surrounding information to guide their predictions.
LLMs have real capabilities. They can write, explain, summarise, translate, code and perform reasoning tasks.
Fluency is not proof. A professional-sounding answer may contain an unsupported claim.
Reasoning can be strong but fallible. Check important calculations, assumptions and conclusions.
Verification requires evidence. An answer becomes more trustworthy when appropriate reliable sources or records actually support it.
Responsible users know when to check. A creative draft and a financial claim do not require exactly the same review process.
Quick Glossary

rows: Computer systems designed to perform tasks associated with intelligent behaviour
A model trained to process and generate language
Adjusting model parameters using data and a learning objective
A small unit of text processed by a language model
The input or instruction given to an AI model
The information available to the model when producing its response
Working through information to solve problems or draw conclusions
Incorrect, fabricated or unsupported model-generated information
Checking whether a claim is supported by reliable evidence
An external function or system an AI application can use when appropriately connected

blocks.text: Useful Technical References
For further learning, explore:
Google — Transformers and Large Language Models
Microsoft — LLM Fundamentals
OpenAI — Does ChatGPT Tell the Truth?
These references provide further explanations of how language models work, what they can do and why factual accuracy requires care.
Complete the questions to test your understanding of the lesson.
Each question has four choices and exactly one correct answer.
For independent practice, read the question and choose an answer before looking at the explanation.

Each question also serves as a flashcard record: the exact question and its four options form the front; the correct letter, full answer and explanation form the back. No separate flashcard questions are needed.
Question 1. What is a Large Language Model?
A. A database that stores only verified information.
B. An AI model trained to process and generate language using learned patterns.
C. A search engine that always retrieves information from live websites.
D. A computer program that can only repeat complete sentences from its training data.
Correct answer: B — An AI model trained to process and generate language using learned patterns.
Explanation: An LLM uses patterns learned during training to process inputs and generate responses. Its abilities can include writing, explanation, translation and reasoning.
Feedback for incorrect answers:
A: A language model is not a database containing only verified facts.
C: Some AI applications can search the web, but web access is not an automatic property of an LLM.
D: An LLM can produce novel combinations of language and solve tasks beyond repeating memorised sentences.
Question 2. What is the main purpose of training an LLM?
A. To make the model automatically aware of every future event.
B. To guarantee that the model never makes factual mistakes.
C. To adjust its numerical parameters so it learns patterns useful for tasks such as language prediction.
D. To store every training document as a separate searchable file.
Correct answer: C — To adjust its numerical parameters so it learns patterns useful for tasks such as language prediction.

Explanation: Training changes a model's internal numerical parameters so it becomes better at its learning objectives. Modern LLMs commonly use next-token prediction during pretraining and may undergo additional training to improve assistant behaviour.
Feedback for incorrect answers:
A: Training cannot automatically provide knowledge of future events.
B: Training improves capabilities but does not guarantee factual correctness.
D: Model training is not equivalent to building an ordinary searchable document archive.
Question 3. What is a token in an LLM?
A. A small unit of text, which may be a word, part of a word or punctuation.
B. A complete paragraph that must contain at least five sentences.
C. A verified fact stored permanently in the model.
D. A special internet connection used to download documents.
Correct answer: A — A small unit of text, which may be a word, part of a word or punctuation.
Explanation: Language models process text using tokens. Token boundaries depend on the model's tokenisation method.
Feedback for incorrect answers:
B: A token does not have to be a paragraph or a complete sentence.
C: Tokens represent pieces of input or output, not verified facts.
D: A token is not an internet connection or document-retrieval mechanism.
Question 4. Why does context matter when an LLM generates an answer?
A. Context automatically verifies the truth of everything in the response.
B. Context forces the model to use exactly the same words every time.
C. Context removes the need to review the generated output.
D. Context gives the model surrounding information that helps it determine suitable responses.
Correct answer: D — Context gives the model surrounding information that helps it determine suitable responses.
Explanation: The model uses available context to interpret the request and generate relevant continuations. More relevant context can improve the answer, but it cannot guarantee correctness.
Feedback for incorrect answers:
A: Context can contain incorrect or incomplete information.
B: Models can produce different answers even with the same context.
C: Context does not eliminate factual or reasoning errors.
Question 5. Which task is primarily an example of language generation rather than factual verification?
A. Confirming whether a real customer received a refund.
B. Writing a fictional birthday greeting in a friendly tone.
C. Checking the current price of a specific airline ticket.
D. Determining whether a real parcel has left a warehouse.
Correct answer: B — Writing a fictional birthday greeting in a friendly tone.
Explanation: A fictional greeting mainly requires suitable language. The other tasks involve real-world facts that need appropriate evidence.
Feedback for incorrect answers:
A: Refund status should be checked against an authorised payment or refund record.
C: Current ticket pricing requires reliable and sufficiently recent information.
D: Real shipment status must be established from appropriate shipping information.
Question 6. An AI assistant solves a supplied arithmetic problem correctly. What does this demonstrate most directly?
A. That the model has verified every fact in the world.
B. That all future answers from the model will be correct.
C. That the model has successfully performed the calculation in this particular case.
D. That the model must have accessed an external database.
Correct answer: C — That the model has successfully performed the calculation in this particular case.
Explanation: A correct solution provides evidence of success on that problem. It does not prove universal accuracy or show which internal or external methods were used.
Feedback for incorrect answers:
A: Solving one problem does not verify unrelated factual information.
B: Correct performance on one task cannot guarantee future performance.
D: A model may perform arithmetic without retrieving information from an external database.
Question 7. An AI claims that a customer's package was delivered yesterday, but no shipping information was supplied. What is the best next action?
A. Check the authorised delivery record before confirming the claim.
B. Tell the customer the package definitely arrived because the AI sounded confident.
C. Ask the AI to repeat its answer and treat agreement as proof.
D. Add more polite language to the claim and send it.
Correct answer: A — Check the authorised delivery record before confirming the claim.
Explanation: The shipping claim requires evidence from an appropriate source. Without that evidence, it remains unverified.
Feedback for incorrect answers:
B: Confidence does not establish delivery status.
C: Repeating a claim does not independently verify it.
D: Polite wording cannot correct an unsupported factual statement.
Question 8. What is an AI hallucination?
A. A model producing several different but acceptable creative stories.
B. A model translating a sentence into another language.
C. A model asking for clarification when necessary information is missing.
D. A model generating inaccurate, fabricated or unsupported information as part of its answer.
Correct answer: D — A model generating inaccurate, fabricated or unsupported information as part of its answer.
Explanation: Hallucinations include invented references, incorrect dates and unsupported factual claims. A response may sound completely natural while containing these errors.
Feedback for incorrect answers:
A: Variation in creative writing is not necessarily a factual error.
B: Translation is an ordinary language-model capability.
C: Requesting clarification can help avoid unsupported assumptions.
Question 9. Which statement about LLM reasoning is most accurate?
A. Language models are incapable of solving any reasoning problem.
B. Language models can perform reasoning tasks, but their reasoning and conclusions may be incorrect.
C. Every answer produced by a language model is logically valid.
D. A model can reason correctly only when every answer has already been stored word for word.
Correct answer: B — Language models can perform reasoning tasks, but their reasoning and conclusions may be incorrect.
Explanation: Modern LLMs can solve complex problems, compare alternatives and develop multi-step explanations. However, they can make logical mistakes or rely on unsupported assumptions.
Feedback for incorrect answers:
A: LLMs demonstrate useful reasoning abilities across many tasks.
C: Generated reasoning must not automatically be assumed correct.
D: Models can solve new problems without retrieving an identical stored answer.
Question 10. An AI assistant provides a website link as evidence for a factual claim. What should you do before treating the claim as verified?
A. Accept the claim because any website link counts as proof.
B. Accept the claim if the website has a professional design.
C. Check that the source exists, is relevant and supports the specific claim.
D. Assume the claim is false because AI-generated answers cannot contain valid sources.
Correct answer: C — Check that the source exists, is relevant and supports the specific claim.
Explanation: Reliable verification requires evaluating the evidence itself. A citation may be incorrect, outdated, fabricated or unrelated to the statement.
Feedback for incorrect answers:
A: A link alone does not prove anything about the claim.
B: Professional design is not a reliable test of factual accuracy.
D: AI answers can contain valid, useful references. They still require appropriate review.
Question 11. You ask an AI for the reason a customer cancelled a subscription. The cancellation record contains no reason. Which response is most responsible?
A. "The customer definitely cancelled because the service was too expensive."
B. "The subscription is cancelled, but the available record does not state the reason."
C. "The customer probably moved to another provider, so we should record that as the reason."
D. "The model has enough general knowledge to identify the customer's personal reason."
Correct answer: B — "The subscription is cancelled, but the available record does not state the reason."
Explanation: This response accurately separates the known cancellation status from the unknown cause. It does not invent a reason.
Feedback for incorrect answers:
A: There is no evidence that cost caused the cancellation.
C: A possible explanation should not be recorded as an established fact.
D: General model knowledge cannot establish an individual customer's undisclosed decision.
Question 12. Two AI assistants independently produce the same answer to a historical question. What can you safely conclude from their agreement alone?
A. The historical answer must be correct.
B. Both assistants have necessarily consulted an official historical archive.
C. The answer no longer requires factual verification.
D. The assistants agree, but their agreement alone does not establish factual correctness.
Correct answer: D — The assistants agree, but their agreement alone does not establish factual correctness.
Explanation: Different models can share similar learned information and errors. Independent, relevant historical evidence is still needed to verify the claim.
Feedback for incorrect answers:
A: Agreement does not guarantee accuracy.
B: Similar answers do not demonstrate that a particular source was consulted.
C: Agreement may support further investigation but does not replace verification.
Question 13. An AI product can use an authorised company database tool. Which statement is most accurate?
A. The assistant may retrieve relevant records through the tool, but the results and final answer still require appropriate interpretation.
B. The language model automatically has access to every private database.
C. A connected tool guarantees that every generated answer will be correct.
D. The model must have memorised all current database records during training.
Correct answer: A — The assistant may retrieve relevant records through the tool, but the results and final answer still require appropriate interpretation.

Explanation: Tools can give AI applications access to information or actions that the standalone model does not possess. Permissions, tool reliability, data quality and interpretation all remain important.
Feedback for incorrect answers:
B: Access requires an appropriate connection and authorisation.
C: Tools and models can both produce or contribute to errors.
D: Retrieving current records through a tool is different from learning information during model training.
Question 14. A company wants an AI to draft a customer message about a delayed refund. Which instruction best reduces unsupported claims?
A. "Give a convincing explanation, even if the records are incomplete."
B. "Write confidently and do not mention uncertainty."
C. "Use only the provided facts, do not invent the reason or arrival date, and explain that the status must be checked."
D. "Assume the refund has been completed because most refunds are eventually completed."
Correct answer: C — "Use only the provided facts, do not invent the reason or arrival date, and explain that the status must be checked."
Explanation: This instruction clearly defines the evidence boundary and directs the model not to invent missing details. The final output should still be reviewed.
Feedback for incorrect answers:
A: Convincing unsupported explanations can mislead customers.
B: Suppressing uncertainty can create false confidence.
D: A general expectation does not establish an individual refund's status.
Question 15. Which statement best describes responsible use of an LLM at work?
A. Every AI output should be rejected because some models make mistakes.
B. Use the model for suitable tasks, review its output, and verify important claims using reliable evidence.
C. Trust any AI answer that is written in clear professional English.
D. Use the model without reviewing its output because training guarantees correctness.
Correct answer: B — Use the model for suitable tasks, review its output, and verify important claims using reliable evidence.
Explanation: Responsible AI use combines useful model capabilities with human judgement. The level of review should match the task and the possible consequences of errors.
Feedback for incorrect answers:
A: Model limitations do not remove their practical value.
C: Professional wording does not prove factual accuracy.
D: Training cannot guarantee that every generated statement is correct.

sections.title: 16. Final Application: Your First AI Support Decision

blocks.text: Imagine that you have joined a customer support team.
A colleague tells you:
I used an AI assistant to draft this customer response. The writing looks excellent, so I think we can send it immediately.
The draft includes a refund amount, a processing date and a promise that the customer will receive the money tomorrow.
You do not know whether anyone has checked the payment records.
Your task: Explain how you would respond to your colleague and what checks you would make before sending the message.
Hint: Appreciate the useful writing, but separate communication quality from factual verification.
Example Professional Response
The AI has helped us prepare a clear message, which is useful.
However, before sending it, we should check the refund amount, processing status and expected payment timing against authorised records.
Good writing does not automatically mean the information is correct.
Why This Response Works
It shows that you understand both the power and the limitations of an LLM.
You are not rejecting the technology.
You are using it intelligently, recognising where its strengths are useful and where evidence is necessary.
You also protect the customer from incorrect promises and help your organisation communicate responsibly.
Final Self-Assessment
You have successfully applied this lesson if you can:
Explain what an LLM is in simple English.
Describe how learned patterns and context influence generated text.
Identify useful language-model capabilities.
Recognise that reasoning can be useful but imperfect.
Detect claims that are unsupported by the available information.
Choose appropriate evidence before relying on consequential facts.
Prepare responsible customer communications without inventing information.
The principle to carry forward is simple:
An LLM can help you produce an answer. Reliable evidence helps you decide whether a factual answer should be trusted.
Lesson End

cases.title: Case 1 — Travelling
context: The children packed their bags and went to the ...
cases.explanation: Airport is a plausible place to go with packed bags. The sentence suggests that the children are travelling or preparing for a journey.
feedback: Good choice. It fits the grammar and travel context.
Incorrect in this sentence. "Hungry" is an adjective, not a suitable destination after "went to the".
Incorrect. "Carefully" is an adverb and does not fit the grammatical structure.
cases.hint: Look for a place someone could visit after packing bags.
cases.note: Important: Airport is the strongest of these three options, but many other destinations could also be reasonable.

cases.title: Case 2 — Business Communication
context: Please attach the signed document to your ...
cases.explanation: The sentence describes attaching a document. Email is a suitable place to attach a digital document.
feedback: Incorrect. An adjective alone does not complete the sentence appropriately.
Correct. It fits the grammar and business context.
Incorrect. Yesterday is a time expression and does not fit here.
cases.hint: Where might you attach a digital document before sending it?

cases.title: Case 3 — Arriving at a Meeting
context: The meeting starts at nine, so please arrive ...
cases.explanation: Earlier is a suitable continuation because the speaker wants the listener to arrive before the meeting starts.
feedback: Correct. It is grammatically and contextually suitable.
Incorrect. Purple is usually a colour and does not appropriately describe when someone should arrive.
Incorrect. Sandwich is a noun and does not fit this request.
cases.hint: Look for a word related to time.

cases.title: Case 1 — Missing Shipping Evidence
context: A customer asks whether an order has shipped.
options: Approve the answer because it is confident.
Ask the AI the same question again and accept its reply.
Check the authorised order record before replying.
cases.explanation: Without an authorised shipping record, the delivery claim is unsupported. Checking the record can establish whether a shipment event actually occurred.
feedback: Incorrect. Confident wording cannot establish shipping status.
Incorrect. Repeating a question is not an independent check.
Correct. An authorised order record can provide evidence of shipping status.
cases.hint: Which action provides information that the AI has not already been given?

cases.title: Case 2 — Rewriting a Thank-You Note
context: You ask the AI to rewrite a fictional thank-you note.
It produces a polite, clear message without adding facts.
options: Review its tone and wording, then use it.
Demand live internet evidence for every adjective.
Assume the draft is necessarily inaccurate.
cases.explanation: This is primarily a writing task. You should review the message for quality and suitability, but independent factual research is generally unnecessary when the fictional text contains no real-world factual claims.
feedback: Correct. Review whether the message meets your communication needs.
Incorrect. External evidence is not needed simply to judge the tone of a fictional message.
Incorrect. The draft may be useful and appropriate without external verification.
cases.hint: Is the task about confirming a real-world fact or creating suitable wording?

cases.title: Case 3 — An Unverified Cancellation Fee
context: The AI gives a confident answer about a company's current cancellation fee.
However, the company policy has not been checked.
options: Publish it because the amount sounds reasonable.
Check the current official policy before quoting a fee.
Ask the AI to sound even more certain.
cases.explanation: Financial claims can affect customer decisions. You should check a reliable current policy, including any relevant conditions.
feedback: Incorrect. A reasonable-sounding amount can still be wrong.
Correct. The current official policy is appropriate evidence.
Incorrect. Stronger wording cannot make an unsupported claim more reliable.
cases.hint: Which action helps establish the actual company rule?

overview: By the end of this lesson, you will understand what a Large Language Model (LLM) is, how it produces answers, what it can do well, and why a convincing answer is not always a correct answer.
You will practise using AI for everyday tasks, recognising unreliable information, making better decisions, and explaining AI confidently to someone who has never used it.
